human_tolerance.notes: "It is a generalist, capable of living in urban, suburban, or rural environments." It roosts in mines, caves, tunnels, buildings, bat boxes, tree cavities, storm drains, wood piles and rock crevices; forages in cities around street lamps; most hibernating individuals are found in warm man-made structures; and in modern human-dominated landscapes many maternity colonies are in buildings rather than the tree cavities where they historically nested.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Mating season is in the fall, shortly before the annual hibernation; some hibernating individuals mate during temporary arousal.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: Hibernation begins around November, often within 80 km of the summer roost, either alone or in small groups, and ends in the spring. It tolerates cold well and makes large brown-fat deposits for arousing quickly, which it reduces to less than half in summer.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Pregnant females separate into maternity colonies around April, of 5-700 individuals but frequently 25-75 adults in the eastern United States and Canada. In the eastern United States twins are commonly born between May and July; western females bear a single pup. Pups are born blind, helpless and 3 g, gaining up to 0.5 g a day, nurse for about a month, and fledge at three to five weeks.

vocalizations.description: The echolocation call, emitted out into the environment with the return echoes read for distance, and for an object's size, shape, density and whether it is moving. It is how the bat navigates and detects the night-flying insects it takes on the wing, and it lets the species hunt where insects are abundant and fewer species compete.

external.note: NCBI taxon id via Wikidata P685.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern (Q211005). The article adds that it 'is evaluated as the lowest conservation priority by the IUCN' and that, unlike other bats in its range, it is relatively resistant to white-nose syndrome and some populations have even increased.

range.note: From southern Canada and Alaska south to Colombia and Venezuela, documented in both Greater and Lesser Antilles - Cuba, Hispaniola, Dominica, Barbados and the Bahamas - and recorded from 300-3,100 m. No introduced range is described. Not treated as introduced anywhere.

traits.limb_count.note: A bat with a 10 mm hind leg and a uropatagium spanning the hind limbs; the schema counts walking limbs plus wings for birds, and this record counts the bat's four limbs consistently with the four-legged mammals in this repository.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Fly and glide are the bat's normal modes; hover covers the stationary or near-stationary hunting it does around street lamps and against vegetation. The record does not claim Climb, which the schema's pose vocabulary could not carry anyway.

traits.thermoregulation.note: An endotherm with large brown-fat deposits for arousing quickly from hibernation and reducing them to less than half in summer.

traits.nest_type.note: Roosts in cavities - mines, caves, tunnels, tree cavities and rock crevices - though it is sometimes found under exfoliating bark, and maternity colonies in human-dominated landscapes are frequently inside buildings.

traits.perching.note: Hangs head-down from a roost, which is not perching on a branch or structure the way a bird does; set to false, matching the treatment of the rodents in this repository.

traits.senses.note: Echolocation is described in some detail - it reads distance, size, shape, density and direction of movement from returning echoes - so hearing is High. The article gives nothing on vision or smell, so those are omitted rather than guessed, even though bats are not blind.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg; at 16.46 g the schema's Tiny band (< 0.05 kg) applies.

traits.mass_kg.note: EltonTraits MamFuncDat BodyMass-Value 16.46 g, inside Wikipedia's 15-26 g band and close to its light end.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of Wikipedia's 110-130 mm adult body length. The schema wants nose or beak tip to tail tip; the article gives body length and tail (47-52 mm) separately, and body length is the figure used because it is what the source labels as such.

traits.lifespan_y.note: A 2011 study of a Colorado population found 'an average life expectancy [of] a little over 6.5 years', which is what the schema's typical-wild figure asks for; some banded bats have lived up to 20 years and males live longer than females.

traits.diet.note: EltonTraits Diet-Inv 100 with every other food class 0, matching 'Big brown bats are insectivorous' and the article's finding that beetles were present in 99.2% of fecal samples. The regional variation it notes - moths added in Oregon, caddisflies and flies in British Columbia - is variation within insects, so it does not change the fraction.

traits.social.note: Maternity colonies of 5-700, 'though in the eastern US and Canada, they are frequently 25-75 adults', and in summer males are most often solitary though they may form small all-male colonies. The group-size ceiling of 75 is the eastern figure the article gives, which is the relevant one for a Michigan locale; a single number cannot carry both the solitary male and the 700-strong colony maximum.

traits.activity_pattern.note: EltonTraits Activity-Nocturnal 1 with Diurnal and Crepuscular 0, and 'The big brown bat is nocturnal, roosting in sheltered places during the day' agree exactly.

traits.defense.note: Flee: it has few natural predators and predation on it is opportunistic, so its response is simply to be airborne and away. The schema has no bite or freeze option that would fit better.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 0.2. It forages around street lamps in cities and roosts inside buildings and bat boxes, so people are routine rather than alarming; it still drops from the roost and darts off at a close approach.

habitat.use.note: EltonTraits ForStrat-Value 'A' gives the aerial stratum as primary, which fits an animal that hunts night-flying insects on the wing; the small arboreal and ground shares cover the tree cavities, wood piles and rock crevices it roosts in and the ground it flies low over. No source quantifies the split.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: "They generally roost in cavities, though they can sometimes be found under exfoliating bark."

habitat.resources.note: Food is invertebrates at 1.0, matching traits.diet. Nesting weight is entirely on the cavity. shelter, log_pile and perch carry the roost range the article lists - buildings, bat boxes, storm drains, wood piles and rock crevices - and are weighted by judgement.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Exploiter on the article's own word: a 'generalist, capable of living in urban, suburban, or rural environments' that forages around street lamps, roosts in buildings and bat boxes, hibernates mostly in warm man-made structures, and forms maternity colonies in buildings in modern landscapes. impervious_max, dist_building_min_m and light_max are authored judgement on that description and are not quantified in the source; dist_building_min_m is 0 because it roosts inside buildings.

habitat.density_per_ha.note: Judgement: the article reports colony sizes, never a density per unit area. A colony of 25-75 spread over the foraging range a single bat covers at night puts typical at 0.1 per hectare, and min and max are an authored tenfold band either side, following the convention used for turdus-migratorius and sciurus-carolinensis. The importer's body-mass fallback would be an acceptable alternative.

seasonal.strategy.note: "Big brown bats enter into hibernation around November ... and come out of hibernation in the spring." Unlike the raccoon's winter rest, this is genuine hibernation with brown fat built for it, so Hibernation is the right strategy.

seasonal.triggers.note: Authored judgement, flagged as such: the schema requires triggers for a Hibernation strategy and no open source states the weather that starts and ends hibernation for this species. Three weeks below 6 C to enter and a fortnight above 9 C to exit are plausible for a cave- and mine-hibernating bat in a Michigan winter - cold and stable rather than merely freezing - and should be replaced if a sourced figure appears.

seasonal.phases.note: Fall mating shortly before hibernation, November entry and spring emergence with hibernating animals usually within 80 km of the summer roost and alone or in small groups, the brown-fat cycle, maternity colonies forming around April of 5-700 but frequently 25-75 adults in the east, May-July twin births in the eastern United States against single pups in the west, 3 g blind pups gaining up to 0.5 g a day, about a month of nursing and fledging at three to five weeks are all stated in the article.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Juvenile duration is authored: fledging at three to five weeks is 21-35 days, taken at 42 days to cover the period of independence before the young are fully weaned into the roost. The 0.2 scale is close to the source's own figures - a 3 g pup against a 15-26 g adult is 0.12 to 0.20 - rounded up for a grown but still young animal.

vocalizations.note: The echolocation call and what it reads - distance, size, shape, density and direction of movement - are the article's own, and the account of why it uses the call (insects are out with fewer predators, less competition and fewer bat predators) is quoted from it too. The waveform and frequency are not given anywhere in the source, so freq_hz is deliberately omitted and the one-second cooldown is authored judgement: it is the rate an animal can actually emit, not a figure from the text. The only other vocalization the article mentions is 'unusual vocalizations' as a symptom of rabies, which is a disease sign rather than a call.

look.note: Colours from the Description: reddish-brown glossy dorsal fur with lighter brown ventral fur, and a black, hairless snout, uropatagium and wing membranes with black ears 12-13 mm long, relatively short and rounded-tipped, with rounded tragi. Proportions are authored judgement for a microbat: a very short neck, tiny 0.15 leg ratio for 10 mm hind legs, a short 0.4 tail ratio for the 47-52 mm tail, a stubby snout and a low 1.8 wing aspect, which is what gives a bat wing its shape against a bird's. The schema has no bat body plan, so the record uses biped_winged and says so here: the model reads as a small dark-membraned winged mammal rather than a bird, with the ear parts carrying the diagnostic rounded black ears. No open source describes the eye colour, so eye is a judgement value. The pose vocabulary has no 'hover' entry even though the behaviour program's hunt gait is hover, so the hover animation is not declared and the host falls back to its fly cycle.

behavior.note: Params for the species' own fsm-aerial-insectivore-v1 program, which ships with this record because no shared program fits a nocturnal flying insectivore that hunts on the wing and hangs up by day. food_m 12 m is the distance at which echolocation resolves a beetle-sized target, hunt_gait hover because the bat takes insects while hovering or aerial-picking rather than walking to them, drink_m 30 m from the day's notes that it comes down to water, and flee_m 15 m and calm_m 40 m are set for an animal with few predators that reacts to a hand rather than to a distant approach.
